subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Gravitational Waves
description: A short lesson to help you apply Gravitational Waves.

hook.text: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime caused by massive objects accelerating—like two black holes spiraling together.

buildup.text: Einstein predicted them in 1916, but they're incredibly faint. Detecting them seemed impossible for nearly a century.

discovery.text: LIGO detected the first gravitational wave in 2015—from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away.

twist.text: LIGO measures distortions smaller than a proton. Its lasers detect length changes of one ten-thousandth of a proton.

climax.text: Gravitational wave astronomy opened a new window on the universe. We can now 'hear' events invisible to telescopes.

punchline.text: Ripples in spacetime itself. A hundred years from prediction to proof.

quiz.question: What was the source of the first gravitational wave detected by LIGO?
options: Two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away
A supernova explosion in a nearby galaxy
The Big Bang's initial expansion of spacetime

details.summary: Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime caused by accelerating massive objects — especially merging black holes and neutron stars. Predicted by Einstein in 1916, they were first directly detected by LIGO in 2015, opening a completely new way to observe the universe beyond…
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational waves let us observe events invisible to telescopes — merging black holes emit no light. Their detection confirmed a century-old prediction and launched multi-messenger astronomy.
takeaways: Ripples in spacetime from accelerating massive objects
Predicted by Einstein in 1916, detected in 2015
They open a window on events invisible to light

faq.question: Can you feel gravitational waves?
faq.answer: Not from astronomical sources — the waves detected by LIGO stretch and squeeze space by less than a thousandth of a proton's width over 4 km. However, if two black holes merged nearby, the waves would be catastrophically powerful.

faq.question: What future gravitational wave detectors are planned?
faq.answer: LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) will be a space-based detector with million-kilometer arms, sensitive to lower frequencies from supermassive black hole mergers.
